summary:
Adıyaman Province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions: 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. The source inventory contains no Adıyaman-specific carve-out from any of this. The provisions that govern a visitor's exposure in the province are national.

The government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Under that framing a leaked draft omnibus justice reform, the 11th Judicial Package, would enable criminal charges against LGBT people countrywide. Human Rights Watch described it on 29 October 2025 as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades, and Istanbul activists held a press conference against it on 28 October 2025. The measure had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement illustrates that gap. Police stop trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and hold them for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detained woman stated that police took no fines but documented her anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk for anyone whose appearance does not match their passport gender marker.

Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at a women's prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in six provinces demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by an opposition MP on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. A country prison profile prepared with a civil society association and using ILGA World data documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Türkiye's largest city shows how the national rules operate in practice. In 2025 police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT background checks before release. The pattern is not confined to one district or one city: the detention totals in the Kaos GL reporting are national.

Trans victims of violence face the more hostile side of the state's response. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The depth of the regime is historical rather than recent. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 under the Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, when gender reassignment surgery became legal. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents of Adıyaman Province live under the same national provisions as visitors, with the additional exposure of permanent records. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, so there is no statutory complaint to file on those grounds.

Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military.

Legal gender change has been available since 1988, but the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation constrains how it is documented. Following the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, hospitals were barred from recording the "other" option and required to issue e-reports, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Residents deprived of liberty face placement by registered sex, arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Adıyaman-specific source in the inventory, the Wikipedia article on Adıyaman Province, yielded no usable finding on trans safety, enforcement or facilities. Whether GBT identity checks, checkpoint document comparisons or LGBT-related detentions occur in Adıyaman itself is not sourced here; the enforcement evidence available is from Istanbul and from national tallies.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been adopted remains unresolved in this inventory. Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and it had not been passed at that point; no later status is sourced.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 is documented at national level through a Kayseri provincial circular. Its application to hospitals in Adıyaman, and any effect on access to transition care in the province, is not sourced.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is carried as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.
